drhp.business: The Company is engaged in the cultivation, manufacture and sale of tea, operating four tea estates all located in the South Bank of Upper Assam, a region renowned for high-quality Assam teas. Its estates produce CTC and orthodox teas sold to Indian domestic customers and to importers in Germany, the UK, the USA and the Middle East. It runs an integrated plantation-to-manufacturing model and does not purchase bought leaf at any of its factories, retaining full control over cultivation and manufacture; teas are marketed either through auction or private channels.

risks.note: MD&A Risks & Concerns states the tea industry is largely dependent on climatic conditions, with weather patterns playing a critical role in determining overall production; erratic rainfall and temperature swings have become increasingly frequent and adversely affect crop yields, particularly during the peak harvesting season. The Outlook section adds that industry viability continues to be impacted by the escalating impact of extreme climatic conditions, and Opportunities & Threats flags vulnerability to climate change and global warming affecting both yield and quality.
risks.risk: Climate and weather dependence — erratic rainfall and fluctuating ambient temperatures across North East tea-growing regions

risks.note: Fluctuating temperature levels have resulted in the growth and proliferation of pests, thereby increasing the cost of crop protection — a direct, recurring cost headwind on an unhedgeable input.
risks.risk: Rising pest incidence raising crop-protection cost

risks.note: Tea cultivation faces significant challenges from labour availability during peak seasons; any shortage may adversely affect timely plucking, impacting crop quality and crop productivity. The Company employed over 3,538 personnel at its estates and other establishments as on 31st March 2026, so labour is both the key operating input and the key fixed cost.
risks.risk: Labour availability in a labour-intensive plantation model

risks.note: Opportunities & Threats names selling prices that fail to keep pace with rising costs as the industry's key challenge, and the Outlook states profitability is likely to be impacted due to escalation in salaries, wages and other input costs, leading to an increase in overall cost. With no pass-through mechanism at auction, this compresses margin directly.
risks.risk: Cost escalation outpacing realisations — wages plus gas, electricity, fuel, pesticides and fertilizers

risks.note: The tea market is highly sensitive to fluctuations of demand and supply, weather conditions, quality differentials and the intensity of international competition; industry viability is impacted by volatile market dynamics. Teas are sold through auction or private channels, leaving realisations exposed to market clearing prices.
risks.risk: Price volatility and demand-supply sensitivity of the tea market

risks.note: The Company operates in a single segment business — cultivation and manufacture of CTC and orthodox teas — with no change in the nature of business during the year and continued concentration on the core tea business. There is no diversification to absorb a bad crop year or a price downcycle.

All four tea estates are located in the South Bank of Upper Assam, so a single regional weather, pest or labour event affects the entire asset base simultaneously; the report itself notes that North India (Assam and North Bengal) accounts for approximately 83% of the country's total tea production, making the regional exposure structural rather than diversifiable.
risks.risk: Geographic concentration in the South Bank of Upper Assam

risks.note: Teas are sold to prominent importers in Germany, UK, USA and the Middle East, and management states sustained efforts are being made to identify and mitigate trade barriers; the Outlook also names the intensity of international competition as a sensitivity for the market.
risks.risk: Export-market access and trade barriers, plus international competition
